metadata.summary: This article presents the adolescent-specific recommendations from the 2023 International Evidence-Based Guideline for PCOS. It covers diagnosis and identification of adolescents “at risk” of PCOS, assessment of metabolic and psychological concerns, lifestyle and symptom management, and transition to adult care. Infertility is outside its scope, and the document notes that evidence specific to adolescents remains limited.

target_population: adolescents between 10 and 19 years of age with PCOS

associated_therapies: 35 μg ethinyl estradiol plus cyproterone acetate preparations
prevention: Consider these preparations as second-line therapy relative to other COCPs, weighing benefits against adverse effects, including venous thromboembolic risk.
Before prescribing COCPs, consider relative and absolute contraindications, higher weight, and cardiovascular risk factors, and discuss risks individually.

recognition: Gastrointestinal symptoms are generally mild, dose dependent, and self-limiting.
prevention: Beginning with a low dose, increasing by 500 mg every 1–2 weekly, and using extended-release preparations may reduce side effects and improve adherence.

recognition: Risk may be greater in people with diabetes, prior bariatric/metabolic surgery, pernicious anemia, or a vegan diet.
prevention: Consider monitoring vitamin B12 in people with risk factors for low vitamin B12.

toxicities.event: Incomplete development of external genital structures of male fetuses (under virilization)
prevention: Whenever pregnancy is possible, healthcare professionals must counsel women, adolescents, and their parents or guardians about this fetal risk.
Women who can become pregnant should be strongly counseled to use effective contraception, such as an intrauterine device or COCPs.
Cyproterone acetate at doses ≥ 10 mg is not advised because of increased risks, including meningioma.

recognition: The document identifies an increased risk with Finasteride and an increased risk of severe liver toxicity with Flutamide and bicalutamide; it does not specify clinical signs.

prevention: Low-fluence laser appears to reduce associated pain while providing facial hair reduction similar to high-fluence laser.

prophylaxis.recommendation: When anti-androgens are used and pregnancy is possible, women who can become pregnant should be strongly counseled to use effective contraception, such as an intrauterine device or COCPs, to prevent under virilization of male fetuses.
prophylaxis.target_population: Women who can become pregnant while using anti-androgens

conditions.name: PCOS
conditions.description: In adolescents, diagnosis requires both menstrual irregularity defined by time since menarche and clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism, after excluding disorders that resemble PCOS. Adult diagnostic criteria differ.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Menstrual irregularity may occur alongside hirsutism or severe acne. Mild acne and irregular cycles can also occur during normal pubertal development, making diagnosis challenging.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Determine whether cycle irregularity meets an adolescent diagnostic criterion.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Cycles are considered normal during the first-year post menarche. Irregularity is defined as < 21 or > 45 days at 1 to < 3 years post menarche; < 21 or > 35 days, or < 8 cycles per year, from 3 years post menarche to perimenopause; or any cycle > 90 days from 1 year post menarche. Primary amenorrhea by age 15 or > 3 years post thelarche also meets the stated definition.

diagnostic_workup.test: History and physical examination for clinical hyperandrogenism
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify clinical signs and assess their onset and progression.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When assessing possible PCOS or marked or worsening hyperandrogenism.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Severe acne and hirsutism are pertinent adolescent signs. New severe or worsening symptoms warrant investigation for androgen-secreting tumors and ovarian hyperthecosis. A rapid course is particularly relevant when assessing for an androgen-secreting tumor.

diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When biochemical assessment is needed for PCOS diagnosis.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Free testosterone may be estimated with the calculated free androgen index. Validated tandem mass spectrometry is preferred for total testosterone; free testosterone should be assessed by calculation, equilibrium dialysis, or ammonium sulfate precipitation. Direct immunoassays have limited diagnostic accuracy. A cited meta-analysis found sensitivity of 80.3% for calculated free testosterone and 80.2% for the free androgen index, with specificity of 93.3% and 86.4%, respectively.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Provide additional assessment of biochemical hyperandrogenism.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: May be considered if testosterone or free testosterone is not elevated.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: These measures have poorer specificity; the greater age-related decrease in dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate applies only to adult women. Validated tandem mass spectrometry should be used if measurement is needed.

diagnostic_workup.test: Biochemical androgen assessment during COCP use
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess androgen levels when measurement is essential despite current COCP use.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Only if biochemical androgen assessment is imperative in someone taking COCP.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: COCP makes reliable assessment difficult. The document advises withdrawing it for a minimum of three months and arranging other contraception during that period.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess hirsutism using a standardized visual measure.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A score of ≥ 4–6 indicates hirsutism. Cosmetic self-treatment can obscure examination findings; only terminal hairs count toward hirsutism assessment.

diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When this finding is suspected; it is rare in adolescents.
If confirmation is needed despite apparently regular cycles.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Ovarian dysfunction remains possible with regular cycles.

diagnostic_workup.test: Evaluation for other causes of hyperandrogenemia
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Exclude disorders that can resemble PCOS.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Particularly when androgen levels markedly exceed laboratory reference ranges or symptoms develop rapidly.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The differential includes ovarian and adrenal neoplastic growths, congenital adrenal hyperplasia, Cushing’s syndrome, iatrogenic causes, and syndromes of severe insulin resistance; ovarian hyperthecosis is specified after menopause. Some androgen-secreting neoplasms produce only mild to moderate androgen elevations.

diagnostic_workup.test: Pelvic ultrasonography for polycystic ovarian morphology
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess whether ovarian morphology can contribute to diagnosis.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Not recommended for diagnosing PCOS during adolescence.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Definitive adolescent ultrasound criteria are unavailable. Assessment for diagnostic purposes may become appropriate at approximately 8 years postmenarche.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess whether this marker can contribute to diagnosis.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Should not yet be used to diagnose adolescents.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Its potential diagnostic use is discussed for approximately 8 years postmenarche, rather than during adolescence.

diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: At diagnosis in all adolescents with PCOS, with regular assessment thereafter.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The guideline does not specify a preferred dysglycemia test for adolescents because evidence is lacking.

diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: In all adolescents with PCOS; repeat screening according to clinical judgment, life changes, and risk factors.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A cited meta-analysis reported up to a four-fold higher prevalence of depression in adolescents with PCOS than in those without PCOS.

follow_up.schedule: Longitudinal care should continue through a planned transition to adult services; the document does not set a fixed visit interval.
recommended_tests: Repeat depression screening according to clinical judgment, life changes, and risk factors
Monitoring of hirsutism, acne, and female pattern hair loss during treatment
long_term_effects: Increased risk of impaired fasting glucose, impaired glucose tolerance, and type 2 diabetes
Obesity, dysglycemia, dyslipidemia, depression, and subfertility may progress during prolonged gaps in care
follow_up.survivorship_notes: The recommended lifelong health plan includes age-appropriate reproductive education, healthy lifestyles, prevention of excess weight gain, assessment of long-term metabolic risks, and preparation for adult care.

conditions.name: Adolescents “at risk” of PCOS
conditions.description: This designation may apply when an adolescent has features of PCOS but does not meet its full diagnostic criteria; it calls for symptom-directed management and continued reassessment rather than an immediate PCOS diagnosis.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Only one of the two required diagnostic features is present: menstrual irregularity or clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism. The group considered for reassessment also includes adolescents with features predating COCP use, persistent features, or significant weight gain during adolescence.

diagnostic_workup.test: Menstrual history and assessment of clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Establish whether one or both required features of adolescent PCOS are present.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: At initial assessment and during subsequent diagnostic reassessment.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: One feature can support an “at risk” designation. If both menstrual irregularity and hyperandrogenism are subsequently present, PCOS can be diagnosed even before 8 years postmenarche, after other disorders are excluded.

diagnostic_workup.test: Biochemical androgen assessment during COCP use
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Support diagnostic reassessment when androgen measurement is essential.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When assessment is imperative in an adolescent already taking COCP.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: COCP interferes with reliable androgen assessment; withdrawal for a minimum of three months is advised while contraception is managed by another means.

follow_up.schedule: Reassessment is advised at or before full reproductive maturity, 8 years post menarche. The timing should be discussed with the adolescent and family, with evaluation maintained before and after transition to adult care.
recommended_tests: Reassessment of menstrual irregularity and clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism
long_term_effects: Recent data suggest abnormal metabolic profiles in adolescents designated “at risk”
follow_up.survivorship_notes: Ongoing follow-up and management should address current symptoms. A planned transition to adult care is important to avoid disruption of reassessment.

therapies_index.name: lifestyle interventions
approved_indications: Recommended for women with PCOS to improve metabolic health, including central adiposity and lipid profile.
Healthy lifestyles are recommended for adolescents, including those without overweight, to help prevent excess weight gain.
therapies_index.administration: Interventions may involve exercise alone or a multicomponent diet with exercise and behavioral strategies.

therapies_index.name: active lifestyle intervention
approved_indications: Considered alongside metformin when discussing options for PCOS management.
Recommended alongside anti-obesity medications when managing higher weight in adults with PCOS.

therapies_index.name: physical activity
approved_indications: Recommended as part of a healthy lifestyle for adolescents.
therapies_index.administration: Adolescents should aim for at least 60 min of moderate to vigorous intensity physical activity per day, with muscle- and bone-strengthening activities at least three times a week.

therapies_index.name: tailored energy deficit
approved_indications: Could be prescribed when an adolescent aims to lose weight.
therapies_index.administration: Tailor to individual energy requirements, weight, and physical activity levels.

therapies_index.name: COCP
approved_indications: Could be considered for hirsutism and/or irregular menstrual cycles in adolescents with PCOS or at risk of PCOS.
Could be used instead of metformin to manage hirsutism and irregular menstrual cycles in PCOS.
therapies_index.administration: Consider natural estrogen preparations and the lowest effective estrogen dose, such as 20–30 μg of ethinyl estradiol or equivalent. The guideline cannot recommend a particular progestin, estrogen, dose, or combination for PCOS. Use for PCOS is generally off-label.
monitoring: Discuss relative and absolute contraindications and side effects individually, taking higher weight and cardiovascular risk factors into account.
If biochemical androgen assessment is essential during COCP use, withdraw the pill for a minimum of three months and arrange other contraception during that period.

therapies_index.name: 35 μg ethinyl estradiol plus cyproterone acetate preparations
approved_indications: Should be considered second-line relative to other COCPs, after weighing benefits against adverse effects.
therapies_index.administration: 35 μg ethinyl estradiol plus cyproterone acetate.

therapies_index.name: ethinyl estradiol
therapies_index.administration: Mentioned as a COCP component at 20–30 μg or equivalent and in 35 μg ethinyl estradiol plus cyproterone acetate preparations.

therapies_index.name: Progestin only oral contraceptives
approved_indications: May be considered for endometrial protection under general-population guidance; evidence in women with PCOS is limited.

therapies_index.name: metformin
approved_indications: Alone, could be considered for cycle regulation in adolescents with PCOS or at risk of PCOS, acknowledging limited evidence.
Could be used instead of COCP for metabolic indications in PCOS.
therapies_index.administration: Begin at a low dose; 500 mg increments 1–2 weekly and extended-release preparations may improve tolerability and adherence. Suggested maximum daily dose is 2.5 g in adults and 2 g in adolescents. Use for PCOS is generally off-label.
key_toxicities: Mild gastrointestinal adverse effects are generally dose dependent and self-limiting.
Use may be associated with low vitamin B12 levels.
monitoring: Reassess whether continued treatment remains necessary.
Consider vitamin B12 monitoring in people with risk factors for low vitamin B12, including diabetes, post bariatric/metabolic surgery, pernicious anemia, or a vegan diet.

therapies_index.name: COCPs and metformin
approved_indications: The guideline discusses their combined use but reports minimal additional benefit in women with a body mass index < 30 kg/m2; adolescent data are unavailable.

therapies_index.name: anti-androgens
approved_indications: With effective contraception, could be considered for hirsutism in women with PCOS after a suboptimal response to a minimum of 6 months of COCP and/or cosmetic therapy.
therapies_index.administration: Use with effective contraception whenever pregnancy is possible.
key_toxicities: Risk of incomplete development of external genital structures of male fetuses if used during pregnancy.
monitoring: Counsel patients who could become pregnant, and their parents or guardians where applicable, about fetal risk and effective contraception.

therapies_index.name: Spironolactone
approved_indications: Discussed among anti-androgens considered for hirsutism in women with PCOS.
key_toxicities: At 25–100 mg/day, it appears to have a lower risk of adverse effects.

therapies_index.name: Cyproterone acetate
approved_indications: Mentioned as an anti-androgen and as a component of a second-line COCP preparation.
key_toxicities: Doses ≥ 10 mg carry increased risk, including meningioma.

therapies_index.name: Finasteride
approved_indications: Discussed among anti-androgens in the management of PCOS.

therapies_index.name: Flutamide
approved_indications: Discussed among anti-androgens in the management of PCOS.
key_toxicities: Increased risk of severe liver toxicity.

therapies_index.name: bicalutamide
approved_indications: Discussed among anti-androgens in the management of PCOS.
key_toxicities: Increased risk of severe liver toxicity.

therapies_index.name: liraglutide
approved_indications: Could be considered alongside active lifestyle intervention for higher weight in adults with PCOS, following general-population guidelines. No adolescent-specific recommendation was made.

therapies_index.name: semaglutide
approved_indications: Could be considered alongside active lifestyle intervention for higher weight in adults with PCOS, following general-population guidelines. No adolescent-specific recommendation was made.

therapies_index.name: orlistat
approved_indications: Could be considered alongside active lifestyle intervention for higher weight in adults with PCOS, following general-population guidelines. No adolescent-specific recommendation was made.

therapies_index.name: Mechanical laser and light therapies
approved_indications: Should be considered to reduce facial hirsutism and address associated depression, anxiety, and quality of life in women with PCOS. No adolescent-specific recommendation was made.
therapies_index.administration: Women with PCOS may require more laser sessions for hair reduction than women with idiopathic hirsutism. Treatment wavelength and delivery vary with skin and hair color; laser is relatively ineffective for blond, grey, or white hair.
key_toxicities: Low fluence laser is associated with less pain than high fluence laser, while both appear similarly effective for facial hair reduction.
Adverse effects appear limited when treatment is provided by experienced, appropriately qualified providers.

therapies_index.name: intense pulse light (IPL)
approved_indications: Could be considered for mechanical hair removal, although benefits may be less pronounced than with laser treatment. Evidence does not support the efficacy of home-based IPL kits.

therapies_index.name: intrauterine device
approved_indications: Given as an example of effective contraception for someone who could become pregnant while using anti-androgens.

special_populations.considerations: Adolescent diagnosis requires both menstrual irregularity, interpreted according to time since menarche, and clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism after exclusion of conditions that mimic PCOS. Pelvic ultrasound findings of polycystic ovarian morphology and AMH levels should not be used for diagnosis during adolescence. Glycemic status should be assessed at diagnosis, and depression screening should use a regionally validated tool. Ongoing care should address symptoms, metabolic risks, reproductive health and transition to adult services.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: COCP could be considered for hirsutism or irregular cycles; metformin alone could be considered for cycle regulation, although adolescent evidence is limited. The suggested maximum daily metformin dose is 2 g in adolescents.

special_populations.considerations: An adolescent with only menstrual irregularity or hyperandrogenism can be considered at risk rather than diagnosed with PCOS. Symptoms warrant management and longitudinal assessment, with diagnostic reassessment advised at or before 8 years post menarche. Features present before COCP use, persistent features and substantial adolescent weight gain are relevant. PCOS can be diagnosed earlier if both required features subsequently occur.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: COCP could be considered for hirsutism or irregular cycles, and metformin alone could be considered for cycle regulation, acknowledging limited evidence. If biochemical androgen assessment becomes essential during COCP use, COCP should be stopped for a minimum of three months while contraception is provided by another means.

special_populations.population: Adolescents and women with PCOS who are not overweight
special_populations.considerations: At adolescence and other important life stages, care should emphasize healthy habits and prevention of excess weight gain. The document notes that adolescents with normal BMI can have insulin resistance.

special_populations.population: Adolescents and women with PCOS who have higher weight
special_populations.considerations: Weight-related health risks should be discussed sensitively to limit stigma. Higher weight and cardiovascular risk factors should be considered when COCP is prescribed. If an adolescent seeks weight loss, an individualized energy deficit could be prescribed in light of energy needs, weight and physical activity.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: For adults with PCOS and higher weight, liraglutide, semaglutide or orlistat could be considered alongside active lifestyle intervention under general population guidance. No specific adolescent recommendation for anti-obesity medication was made because adolescent data are lacking.

special_populations.population: Women and adolescents who can become pregnant
special_populations.considerations: When anti-androgens are used and pregnancy is possible, patients and, where appropriate, parents or guardians must be counseled about the risk of incomplete development of a male fetus’s external genital structures.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Women who can become pregnant should be strongly counseled to use effective contraception, such as an intrauterine device or COCPs, when receiving anti-androgens.

special_populations.considerations: Adult diagnostic criteria differ from adolescent criteria: diagnosis may be based on at least two of menstrual irregularity or ovulatory dysfunction, clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism, and polycystic ovarian morphology on ultrasound or elevated AMH. Recommendations for adults should not automatically be treated as adolescent-specific recommendations.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: The suggested maximum daily metformin dose is 2.5 g in adults. Anti-obesity medications and cosmetic therapies have adult recommendations, while the document makes no specific adolescent recommendations for these treatments because of insufficient adolescent data.

special_populations.population: First-degree relatives of people with PCOS
special_populations.considerations: First-degree relatives have an increased diabetes risk; healthcare professionals, people with PCOS and their relatives should be aware of this risk and the need for regular glycemic assessment.

special_populations.population: People taking metformin who have risk factors for low vitamin B12
special_populations.considerations: Metformin use may be associated with low vitamin B12, particularly with risk factors such as diabetes, prior bariatric or metabolic surgery, pernicious anemia or a vegan diet; monitoring should be considered.

special_populations.population: Adolescents with PCOS or at risk of PCOS transitioning to adult care
special_populations.considerations: Longitudinal follow-up and a planned transition are important because interruptions in care can occur. Before transition, clinicians and adolescents should discuss comorbidities and develop longer-term health plans that support increasing responsibility for self-care.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Adolescents with PCOS, including those who are not overweight.
decision_rules: Use shared decision-making with the adolescent and parent/s or guardian/s to establish individual concerns and treatment goals.
Focus on a healthy lifestyle and preventing excess weight gain; if weight loss is the adolescent’s goal, an individualized energy deficit could be prescribed.

recommended_regimens.name: Lifestyle interventions
recommended_regimens.summary: Exercise alone, or a multicomponent approach combining diet, exercise and behavioral strategies, is recommended to improve metabolic health, including central adiposity and lipid profile.

recommended_regimens.name: moderate to vigorous intensity physical activity
recommended_regimens.summary: Adolescents should aim to include activities that strengthen muscle and bone.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: At least 60 min per day, with muscle- and bone-strengthening activities at least three times a week.

not_recommended.name: specific type of diet composition
not_recommended.reason: There is no evidence supporting one dietary composition over another for anthropometric, metabolic, hormonal, reproductive or psychological outcomes.

not_recommended.name: specific type and intensity of exercise
not_recommended.reason: Evidence does not support one type or intensity over another for anthropometric, metabolic, hormonal, reproductive or psychological outcomes.

supportive_care: Discuss weight-related health risks sensitively to avoid weight bias and stigma.
Consider increasing family members’ awareness of weight stigma.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Individual preferences and sustainable approaches should guide lifestyle choices; broader family involvement may be relevant. The document describes limited randomized intervention evidence in adolescents.

decision_rules: Address the adolescent’s current symptoms and agree on treatment goals with the adolescent and parent/s or guardian/s without requiring a definitive PCOS diagnosis.
Encourage a healthy lifestyle and prevention of excess weight gain.

recommended_regimens.name: moderate to vigorous intensity physical activity
recommended_regimens.summary: Adolescents should aim for physical activity that includes muscle- and bone-strengthening activities.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: At least 60 min per day, with muscle- and bone-strengthening activities at least three times a week.

supportive_care: Discuss weight-related concerns without reinforcing weight stigma.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Symptom management should accompany longitudinal reassessment of PCOS status. A weight-loss goal, if chosen by the adolescent, may be addressed with an energy deficit tailored to individual requirements, weight and physical activity.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Adolescents with PCOS who have hirsutism and/or irregular menstrual cycles.
decision_rules: Choose treatment according to the presenting symptoms and the adolescent’s preferences.
COCP could be used over metformin when the treatment target is hirsutism or irregular menstrual cycles.
Follow general population prescribing guidance because a specific COCP progestin, estrogen dose or combination cannot currently be recommended.

recommended_regimens.name: COCP
recommended_regimens.summary: Could be considered for hirsutism and/or irregular menstrual cycles. Consider natural estrogen preparations or the lowest effective estrogen dose, balancing efficacy with metabolic risks, adverse effects, cost and availability.

alternative_regimens.name: metformin
alternative_regimens.summary: Could be considered alone to regulate cycles, although adolescent evidence is limited.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Cycle regulation is a treatment goal and the choice reflects individual circumstances and preferences.

response_assessment.method: Monitor hirsutism, acne and female pattern hair loss.
response_assessment.interpretation: Use changes in clinical signs to consider whether treatment needs adjustment.

supportive_care: Discuss cosmetic therapies when addressing the main presenting symptoms.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: COCP use for PCOS is generally off-label. Explain the evidence, potential concerns and adverse effects to adolescents and parent/s or guardian/s. Discuss relative and absolute contraindications individually, including higher weight and cardiovascular risk factors. The document gives 20–30 μg of ethinyl estradiol or equivalent as an example of a low estrogen dose.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Adolescents “at risk” of PCOS who have hirsutism and/or irregular menstrual cycles.
decision_rules: Treatment may address current symptoms while diagnostic status remains under review.
COCP could be considered for hirsutism and/or irregular cycles; metformin alone could be considered for cycle regulation.
Discuss with the adolescent and parent/s or guardian/s how COCP use may affect later biochemical androgen assessment.

recommended_regimens.name: COCP
recommended_regimens.summary: Could be considered for hirsutism and/or irregular menstrual cycles, with prescribing informed by general population guidance and the lowest effective estrogen dose considered.

alternative_regimens.name: metformin
alternative_regimens.summary: Could be considered alone for cycle regulation despite limited evidence.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Cycle regulation is the treatment objective.

response_assessment.method: Monitor clinical signs of hyperandrogenism, including hirsutism, acne and female pattern hair loss.
response_assessment.interpretation: Improvement or a need to adjust treatment should be assessed.

supportive_care: Consider cosmetic therapies according to the adolescent’s main concerns.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: COCP can make biochemical hyperandrogenism difficult to assess. If biochemical androgen testing is imperative while taking COCP, it should be withdrawn for a minimum of three months and contraception managed by another means during that period. Discuss possible withdrawal for diagnostic reassessment, particularly when hyperandrogenism is absent and hypogonadism is possible. Consider contraindications and adverse effects through individualized discussion.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Adolescents with PCOS or “at risk” of PCOS for whom COCP is being selected to manage hirsutism and/or irregular menstrual cycles.
decision_rules: Consider 35 μg ethinyl estradiol plus cyproterone acetate preparations as second-line rather than other COCPs, weighing potential benefits against adverse effects.

recommended_regimens.name: 35 μg ethinyl estradiol plus cyproterone acetate
recommended_regimens.summary: Should be considered a second-line COCP preparation, with attention to venous thromboembolic risk.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Assess COCP contraindications and adverse effects individually. The document does not specify a particular first-line COCP formulation.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Adolescents with PCOS who have metabolic features.
decision_rules: Metformin could be used over COCP when the indication is metabolic.
Discuss the feasibility and effectiveness of active lifestyle intervention when deciding whether to prescribe metformin.

recommended_regimens.name: metformin
recommended_regimens.summary: Could be used instead of COCP for metabolic indications. Begin with a low dose; gradual increases and extended-release preparations may reduce adverse effects and improve adherence.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: Increase by 500 mg every 1–2 weekly; suggested maximum daily dose is 2 g in adolescents.

alternative_regimens.name: active lifestyle intervention
alternative_regimens.summary: Discuss as an active management approach; the document states that metformin and active lifestyle intervention have similar efficacy.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Consider its feasibility and effectiveness through shared decision-making.

supportive_care: Consider monitoring vitamin B12 in those with risk factors for low vitamin B12, including diabetes, post bariatric/metabolic surgery, pernicious anemia or a vegan diet.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Explain that gastrointestinal and other mild adverse effects are generally dose-dependent and self-limiting. Long-term use appears safe on the basis of experience in other populations. The document notes that adolescents with normal BMI can have insulin resistance.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Adolescents “at risk” of PCOS for whom metabolic features or cycle regulation are treatment concerns.
decision_rules: Metformin alone could be considered for cycle regulation, acknowledging limited evidence.
Discuss active lifestyle intervention and individual treatment goals before prescribing.

recommended_regimens.name: metformin
recommended_regimens.summary: Could be considered alone for cycle regulation. The document also discusses its use for metabolic features in adolescents “at risk” of PCOS.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: Increase by 500 mg every 1–2 weekly from a low starting dose; suggested maximum daily dose is 2 g in adolescents.

alternative_regimens.name: active lifestyle intervention
alternative_regimens.summary: Discuss its feasibility and effectiveness; the document describes efficacy similar to metformin.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Selection should reflect shared decision-making and the adolescent’s goals.

response_assessment.method: Reconsider the continuing indication for metformin.

supportive_care: Consider vitamin B12 monitoring when risk factors for low vitamin B12 are present.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Evidence for metformin for cycle regulation in this population is limited. Mild gastrointestinal effects are generally dose-dependent and self-limiting; extended-release preparations may improve tolerability and adherence.

decision_rules: Recommend lifestyle intervention to improve metabolic health.
Select sustainable dietary and physical activity approaches according to individual preferences rather than favoring a specific composition, exercise type or intensity.

recommended_regimens.name: Lifestyle interventions
recommended_regimens.summary: Exercise alone, or a multicomponent combination of diet, exercise and behavioral strategies, is recommended for metabolic health, including central adiposity and lipid profile.

not_recommended.reason: There is no evidence supporting one dietary composition over another for the stated anthropometric, metabolic, hormonal, reproductive or psychological outcomes.

not_recommended.name: specific type and intensity of exercise
not_recommended.reason: Evidence does not support one exercise type or intensity as better than another for the stated outcomes.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: In those who are not overweight, the focus at key life points should be a healthy lifestyle and prevention of excess weight gain.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Adults with PCOS who have hirsutism and/or irregular menstrual cycles.

artifacts.title: Table 4 Adolescent recommendations for the assessment and management of polycystic ovary syndrome. Modified from 2023 Guideline

rows: 1) Criteria required 1a) Menstrual irregularities and ovulatory dysfunction

During the first year after menarche, irregular cycles can be part of normal puberty. Irregularity is defined at 1 to < 3 years post menarche by cycles < 21 or > 45 days; from 3 years post menarche to perimenopause by cycles < 21 or > 35 days or < 8 cycles per year; from 1 year post menarche by any cycle > 90 days; or by primary amenorrhea at age 15 or > 3 years after thelarche. If cycles meet these criteria, consider PCOS and assess it under this Guideline.
Average age at menarche can differ between populations.

Discuss whether and when to assess or diagnose PCOS with adolescents who have irregular cycles and their parent/s or guardian/s, taking account of diagnostic uncertainty and psychosocial and cultural considerations.
Regular cycles do not exclude ovarian dysfunction; serum progesterone may be measured when confirmation of anovulation is needed.
For biochemical hyperandrogenism in PCOS diagnosis, assess total and free testosterone; calculated free androgen index can provide an estimate of free testosterone.

If neither testosterone nor free testosterone is elevated, consider androstenedione and dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate; these are less specific, and dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate declines more with age, with that age-related qualification applying only to adults.

Use validated, highly accurate tandem mass spectrometry assays for total testosterone and, when required, androstenedione and dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate. Assess free testosterone by calculation, equilibrium dialysis or ammonium sulfate precipitation.
Prefer tandem mass spectrometry to direct immunoassays for total or free testosterone because direct assays have limited accuracy, sensitivity and precision for detecting hyperandrogenism in PCOS.
Androgen concentrations reach adult ranges by 12–15 years of age in most adolescents.

COCP makes biochemical hyperandrogenism difficult to assess reliably by increasing sex hormone-binding globulin and suppressing gonadotrophin-dependent androgen production. If testing is essential during COCP use, stop it for a minimum of three months and arrange another form of contraception during that interval.

Markedly elevated androgens warrant consideration of causes other than PCOS: ovarian or adrenal tumors, congenital adrenal hyperplasia, Cushing’s syndrome, ovarian hyperthecosis after menopause, iatrogenic causes and severe insulin resistance syndromes. Some androgen-secreting tumors cause only mild or moderate elevations; symptom onset and rapid progression are therefore important.
Take a comprehensive history and examine for clinical hyperandrogenism: acne, female pattern hair loss and hirsutism in adults, and severe acne and hirsutism in adolescents.
Recognize the possible psychosocial harm of clinical hyperandrogenism and take reports of unwanted excess hair or female pattern hair loss seriously even when visible severity seems low.
An mFG score of ≥ 4–6 identifies hirsutism; self-treatment may obscure its clinical assessment.
Consider ethnic variation in hirsutism severity, while recognizing that its prevalence appears comparable across ethnicities.

Prefer standardized visual assessment of hirsutism, such as mFG alongside a photographic atlas; consider Ludwig or Olsen scales for female pattern hair loss, which is rare in adolescents. No universally accepted visual acne assessment exists. Cosmetic self-treatment can mask hyperandrogenism, and self-reported unwanted hair growth—and possibly acne or hair loss—deserves evaluation even without obvious examination findings. Count terminal hairs for hirsutism; untreated hairs can exceed > 5 mm and differ in shape, texture and pigmentation. Investigate new severe or worsening hyperandrogenism for androgen-secreting tumors and ovarian hyperthecosis. Monitor hirsutism, acne and female pattern hair loss during treatment to assess improvement or the need to adjust therapy.
2) Investigations not recommended for diagnosis of PCOS during adolescence 2a) Ultrasound and polycystic ovary morphology
Do not use ultrasonographic polycystic ovary morphology to diagnose adolescent PCOS because definitive adolescent criteria are unavailable.
Do not yet use AMH in adolescents.

For adolescents with PCOS features who do not fulfill diagnostic criteria, consider an “increased risk” designation and advise reassessment at or before reproductive maturity, 8 years post menarche. This includes features preceding COCP, persistent features and substantial adolescent weight gain.
Inform healthcare professionals and women with PCOS that impaired fasting glucose, impaired glucose tolerance and type 2 diabetes are more likely regardless of age or body mass index.
Assess glycemic status when PCOS is diagnosed in every adult and adolescent.
Ensure healthcare professionals, adults and adolescents with PCOS, and their first-degree relatives understand the increased diabetes risk and the need for regular glycemic assessment.
Recognize that moderate to severe depressive symptoms and depression are common in adults and adolescents with PCOS; screen everyone in these groups for depression using regionally validated tools.
Recognize the high prevalence of moderate to severe anxiety symptoms and anxiety disorders in adults with PCOS, and screen adults using regionally validated tools.
Recognize that PCOS features may adversely affect body image.
Consider eating disorders and disordered eating in PCOS at any weight, particularly during weight management or lifestyle interventions.

Recommend exercise alone or a multicomponent intervention combining diet, exercise and behavioral approaches to all women with PCOS to improve metabolic health, including central adiposity and lipid profile.
For adolescents and at other key life stages without overweight, emphasize healthy habits and prevention of excess weight gain.
Consider that evidence does not favor one dietary composition over another for anthropometric, metabolic, hormonal, reproductive or psychological outcomes.
Consider that evidence does not establish superiority of any exercise type or intensity for anthropometric, metabolic, hormonal, reproductive or psychological outcomes.
Adolescents should aim for at least 60 min of moderate- to vigorous-intensity activity each day, including muscle- and bone-strengthening activities at least three times a week.
Consider promoting awareness of weight stigma among relatives of women and adolescents with PCOS.
Decisions must be shared among the patient, parent/s or guardian/s and healthcare professional.
Elicit and account for personal characteristics, preferences and values when proposing individual or combined interventions.
Before prescribing medication, establish which treatment outcomes matter to each adult or adolescent.

PCOS medications generally lack approval specifically for this indication, so evidence-based prescribing is usually off-label. Explain the evidence, concerns and possible adverse effects to adults, adolescents and their parent/s or guardian/s; regulatory agencies should consider approval of evidence-based PCOS medicines.
Consider COCP for hirsutism and/or irregular cycles in adolescents with diagnosed PCOS or at risk of PCOS.
Consult general-population guidance for COCP prescribing in adults and adolescents with PCOS; no specific progestin or estrogen type, dose or COCP combination can currently be recommended.
Consider 35 μg ethinyl estradiol plus cyproterone acetate as second-line rather than other COCP preparations, weighing benefit against harms including venous thromboembolism.
Progestin-only oral contraceptives may be considered for endometrial protection under general-population guidance; PCOS-specific evidence is limited.
COCP could be preferred to metformin for hirsutism and irregular cycles in PCOS.

When prescribing COCP, address the principal symptoms and consider cosmetic treatments. Share decisions using accurate information about COCP efficacy and safety to support adherence. Consider natural estrogens and the lowest effective estrogen dose, such as 20–30 μg of ethinyl estradiol or equivalent, while weighing efficacy, metabolic risk, adverse effects, cost and availability. Recognize limited PCOS-specific evidence and follow general-population guidance. Discuss contraindications and adverse effects individually, accounting for higher weight and cardiovascular risk factors associated with PCOS.
Metformin alone could be considered for cycle regulation in adolescents with PCOS or at risk of PCOS, while acknowledging limited evidence.

When prescribing metformin, discuss whether active lifestyle intervention is feasible and effective, and explain that the two have similar efficacy. Mild effects, including gastrointestinal effects, are usually dose dependent and self-limiting. A low starting dose, increments of 500 mg every 1–2 weeks and extended-release formulations may improve tolerability and adherence. Suggested maximum daily doses are 2.5 g for adults and 2 g for adolescents. Long-term use appears safe based on other populations, but reassess the need for continued treatment. Consider monitoring vitamin B12 when deficiency risk factors are present, including diabetes, post bariatric/metabolic surgery, pernicious anemia and vegan diet.
Metformin could be preferred to COCP for metabolic indications in PCOS.
With effective contraception, consider anti-androgens for hirsutism in women with PCOS when response remains inadequate after a minimum of 6 months of COCP and/or cosmetic therapy.

When pregnancy is possible, counsel women, adolescents and parent/s or guardian/s that anti-androgens risk incomplete development of male fetal external genitalia. Strongly counsel those who can become pregnant to use effective contraception, such as an intrauterine device or COCP.

When prescribing anti-androgens, consider general-population advice: Spironolactone at 25–100 mg/day appears to carry fewer adverse effects; cyproterone acetate at ≥ 10 mg is not advised because risks include meningioma; Finasteride increases liver-toxicity risk; Flutamide and bicalutamide increase severe liver-toxicity risk. PCOS-specific anti-androgen evidence comes from few small studies.
5) Other medications: anti-obesity medications and inositol
Alongside active lifestyle intervention, liraglutide, semaglutide and orlistat could be considered for higher weight in adults with PCOS under general-population guidance.
Do not currently recommend particular types, doses or combinations of inositol for adults or adolescents with PCOS because quality evidence is lacking.
Consider mechanical laser and light treatments to reduce facial hirsutism and address related depression, anxiety and quality of life in women with PCOS.
Women with PCOS may need more laser sessions for hair reduction than women with idiopathic hirsutism.
Adverse effects appear limited with experienced, appropriately qualified practitioners; encourage women to seek hair-reduction care from such providers.

For laser hair removal, adapt wavelength and delivery to skin and hair color; effectiveness is relatively low for blond, grey or white hair. Adding COCP, with or without anti-androgens, may improve reduction and maintenance compared with laser alone. Low- and high-fluence laser appear similarly effective for facial hair, but low fluence causes less pain.
IPL hair removal could be considered, although its benefit may be smaller than that of laser. Evidence does not support the efficacy of home IPL kits.
Provide everyone with PCOS with tailored, high-quality, culturally appropriate and inclusive information, education and resources.
Treat information, education and resources as a patient priority and deliver them respectfully and empathetically.
Prioritize equitable access to evidence-based primary care, with routes to integrated specialist and multidisciplinary services when needed.
Use shared decision-making and support patients in taking independent action to manage their health and care.
Know about PCOS, apply evidence-based approaches when discussing diagnosis, treatment and health implications, and identify and prioritize the patient’s concerns.

Recommend a reproductive life plan and age-appropriate reproductive-health education for adolescents and women with PCOS, addressing healthy lifestyle, prevention of excess weight gain and optimization of preconception risk factors.

document_sections.heading: Abstract
document_sections.content: Background: Accurate diagnosis of polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), or recognition of adolescents “at risk,” is important for screening, treatment, and lifelong health planning. The 2023 International Evidence-Based Guideline for PCOS sought to improve outcomes through timely diagnosis beginning in adolescence. Methods: Guideline development followed Appraisal of Guidelines for Research and Evaluation (AGREEII) methods. Healthcare professionals and patients or consumers examined evidence addressing 55 prioritized clinical questions. Searches of OVID MEDLINE, All EBM, PsycInfo, EMBASE, and CINAHL extended through August 2022. The Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluation (GRADE) framework informed judgments about evidence and recommendation strength. Results: This manuscript presents the adolescent-specific recommendations. Diagnosis requires both menstrual irregularity, defined by time since menarche, and clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism, after exclusion of disorders resembling PCOS. An adolescent with only one feature can be considered “at risk” and needs symptom management and follow-up. Pelvic ultrasonography findings of polycystic ovarian morphology and anti-Müllerian hormone levels should not establish the diagnosis during adolescence. Recommended lifelong planning encompasses healthy lifestyles, assessment of depression and metabolic features, and transition to adult services, supported by shared decisions and discussion of weight-related risks without weight stigma. Combined oral contraceptive pills are indicated for irregular cycles and clinical hyperandrogenism in adolescents with PCOS or “at risk,” with attention to low-dose preparations; metformin could be considered for metabolic features and cycle regulation. Adolescent evidence remains limited, with recommendations drawing on evidence of low to moderate certainty. Conclusions: International participation and rigorous methods produced adolescent diagnostic criteria distinct from adult criteria and clarified screening and management.

document_sections.heading: Background
document_sections.content: PCOS affects ~ 8% of adolescents. Pubertal menstrual irregularity, acne, and polycystic ovarian morphology (PCOM) overlap with adult diagnostic features: applying those features during adolescence may overdiagnose PCOS, whereas overlooking diagnostic signs may delay or miss diagnosis and have adverse long-term consequences. Individuals have described diagnostic delays despite symptoms beginning in adolescence. The consensus-based Rotterdam criteria were revised into evidence-based criteria in the 2018 and 2023 international guidelines. For adults, the 2023 Guideline requires at least two of menstrual irregularity or ovulatory dysfunction, clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism, and PCOM on ultrasound or elevated anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH); PCOM and AMH are unsuitable diagnostic criteria during adolescence. The 2023 update aimed to provide evidence-based diagnosis, assessment, and treatment recommendations from adolescence through adulthood. This manuscript concentrates on its adolescent recommendations and supporting evidence. “Adolescent” denotes ages 10 to 19 years under the World Health Organization definition; certain recommendations also identify women within 8 years postmenarche, or a gynecological age of 8 years or less.

document_sections.heading: Methods
document_sections.content: Development, revision, and expansion followed international guideline methods and the Appraisal of Guidelines for Research and Evaluation (AGREE II) process. Searches of OVID MEDLINE, All EBM, PsycInfo, EMBASE, and CINAHL ran until August 2022. Evidence synthesis included integrity checks using the Research Integrity in Guideline Development framework, including the Research Integrity Assessment and Trustworthiness in Randomized Controlled Trials checklist. An international advisory board, project board, and five guideline development groups (GDGs) engaged 80 members from 39 organizations across six continents (71 countries) over 12 months. Participants included people with PCOS and multidisciplinary clinical, allied-health, and research experts throughout development. The groups addressed 55 questions through 52 systematic reviews and three narrative reviews. Using Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluation (GRADE), they judged risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, and other factors; evidence certainty ranged from very low to high. Recommendation categories followed the GRADE evidence-to-decision framework. Partner societies and the public reviewed draft recommendations internationally; changes required supporting evidence. The Australian National Health and Medical Research Council approved the final Guideline, which participating societies endorsed. Tables 1 and 2 describe evidence certainty and recommendation strength, while Table 3 explains the recommendation categories.

document_sections.heading: Results
document_sections.content: The complete 2023 Guideline addresses screening, diagnosis and risk assessment; psychological features; lifestyle; management of nonfertility features; and infertility. This manuscript summarizes 63 adolescent recommendations in Table 4 but excludes infertility. Table 3 distinguishes evidence-based recommendations (EBR), made when evidence is sufficient; consensus recommendations (CR), informed by general-population evidence when adequate PCOS evidence is unavailable; and practice points (PP), addressing important issues for which evidence was not sought. Table 4 organizes adolescent assessment and management recommendations by topic, category, and grade or quality.

document_sections.heading: Screening, diagnostic, and risk assessment
document_sections.content: Adolescent PCOS diagnosis requires menstrual irregularity together with hyperandrogenism after conditions that resemble PCOS have been excluded. The following diagnostic discussion considers menstrual patterns, biochemical and clinical hyperandrogenism, investigations unsuitable in adolescence, adolescents “at risk,” and associated health risks.

document_sections.heading: 1) Diagnostic criteria required
document_sections.content: Both defined menstrual irregularity and hyperandrogenism are required for adolescent diagnosis, following exclusion of disorders that mimic PCOS.

document_sections.heading: 1a) Menstrual irregularities
document_sections.content: The updated search on when postmenarcheal irregular cycles indicate persistent dysfunction found no studies meeting its selection criteria. Definitions by years since menarche therefore remained unchanged and draw on the natural history of cycles and ovulation in healthy adolescents. Physiological maturation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis can cause irregular cycles during the early postmenarcheal years, making the precise point at which irregularity signals PCOS uncertain. By the third postmenarcheal year, 95% of cycles had an average adult length of 28 days (range 24–35 days). Accordingly, menstrual irregularity defined in relation to time after menarche constitutes one of the two necessary adolescent diagnostic features. Table 4 specifies the cycle definitions and accompanying recommendations.

document_sections.heading: 1b) Hyperandrogenism: biochemical and/or clinical
document_sections.content: An updated search on biochemical assessment found 17 studies, including two studies with 249 adolescents; most (n = 11) assessed total testosterone and the free androgen index (FAI). A meta-analysis supporting four evidence-based recommendations found that calculated free testosterone and FAI performed best among the compared androgens for diagnosing hyperandrogenism: sensitivity was 80.3% and 80.2%, respectively, and specificity was 93.3% and 86.4%, respectively. Total testosterone, androstenedione, and dehydroepiandrosterone had sensitivity of approximately 70% and specificity of approximately 75–85%; the manuscript says these are not routinely recommended for diagnosis. The updated search on clinical identification located seven studies, none involving adolescents, with substantial heterogeneity. Adolescent clinical recommendations were therefore consensus recommendations. Mild acne is frequent in adolescence, whereas severe acne around menarche is uncommon and more suggestive of hyperandrogenism. Modified Ferriman-Gallwey thresholds came from adult studies. Table 4 sets out the biochemical and clinical assessment recommendations and their grades.

document_sections.heading: 2) Investigations not recommended for adolescent PCOS diagnosis.
document_sections.content: Pelvic ultrasound assessment of PCOM and AMH levels are not recommended to diagnose PCOS until 8 years postmenarche, when the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis is considered mature and evidence-based PCOM diagnostic criteria are available. Normative ultrasound and serum observations show rapid adolescent increases in ovarian size and follicle populations, reaching a peak in early adulthood (20 years). These changing features make adult PCOM definitions inappropriate during adolescence. Although pooled evidence suggests some adolescent diagnostic value for ovarian volume and AMH, its limitations include small samples, emphasis on older adolescents, differing imaging methods or assays, and variable definitions of adolescent PCOS.

document_sections.heading: 3) Adolescents “at risk” of PCOS
document_sections.content: An adolescent with only one of the two necessary diagnostic features—menstrual irregularity or ovulatory dysfunction, or hyperandrogenism—should be regarded as “at risk” of PCOS and evaluated longitudinally. Table 4 describes reassessment for adolescents with suggestive features who do not yet meet diagnostic criteria.

document_sections.heading: 4) Other risks associated with PCOS
document_sections.content: Adult PCOS is associated with cardiovascular disease, impaired glucose tolerance or type 2 diabetes, obstructive sleep apnea, endometrial hyperplasia, and cancer; in adolescents, the identified association is an increased risk of impaired glucose tolerance or type 2 diabetes. Studies comparing dysglycemia tests involved adults, not adolescents. In those adult studies, the 75 oral glucose tolerance test was the most accurate assessment regardless of body mass index (BMI); adult guidance also allowed consideration of fasting plasma glucose and/or glycated hemoglobin if that test was unavailable, while noting reduced accuracy. Because adolescent evidence was absent, the Guideline did not recommend a particular adolescent dysglycemia test. First-degree relatives of people with PCOS also have increased diabetes risk. Table 4 contains the related risk-awareness and glycemic-assessment recommendations.

document_sections.heading: Psychological features
document_sections.content: Four evidence-based recommendations address psychological features. Depression screening is supported by a meta-analysis of 47 studies, including six studies with 1098 adolescents, that found depression prevalence up to a four-fold higher in adolescents with PCOS than in those without it. Generic online screening resources are available; screening and repeat screening should reflect clinical judgment, life events, and risk factors. A qualitative synthesis found that adolescents experienced symptoms being normalized or dismissed, insufficient discussion of options, follow-up overly centered on future fertility, and neglect of immediate concerns. Healthcare professionals should improve shared decision-making, communication of medical news, and support for adolescent participation in care. For anxiety, a meta-analysis of 27 studies, including 3 studies with 455 adolescents, found greater prevalence in adults with PCOS than in adult comparators, but the small adolescent evidence did not reflect that finding. Few adolescent studies of negative body image and eating disorders have shown higher prevalence with PCOS than in controls. Clinicians should nevertheless recognize the limited adolescent research, adult associations, and the occurrence of these concerns in adolescents without PCOS. Table 4 presents the psychological recommendations and grades.

document_sections.heading: Lifestyle
document_sections.content: Excess weight and weight gain are common population concerns and are exacerbated in adolescents and adults with PCOS in an obesogenic environment. Obesity and excessive gain adversely affect reproductive, metabolic, and psychological health and can be especially difficult while adolescent self-image is developing. Weight-related risks should be discussed sensitively to avoid bias and stigma; healthcare professionals should also consider requesting permission before measuring weight. Lifestyle interventions have shown benefits in adolescents, although randomized trials are too limited to establish best practice. Based on population evidence, every adolescent, including those without overweight, is recommended to maintain healthy habits and avoid excess weight gain. If an adolescent seeks weight loss, an individually tailored energy deficit could be prescribed with attention to energy requirements, weight, and activity. The evidence-based recommendations do not favor one diet or exercise approach over another; general-population strategies should instead accommodate sustainable personal preferences and broader family involvement. The consensus recommendation on exercise duration also derives from population guidance. Table 4 provides the specific lifestyle recommendations.

document_sections.heading: Management of nonfertility features
document_sections.content: Whether an adolescent has established PCOS or is “at risk,” treatment should respond to that person's concerns. First, the adolescent, parents or guardians, and clinician should discuss treatment aims, lifestyle changes, the evidence-based but generally “off-label” use of combined oral contraceptive pills (COCP) and metformin for PCOS, and other possible interventions. COCP could be considered for hirsutism and/or irregular cycles in adolescents with PCOS or “at risk,” on the basis of 10 studies (420 adolescents). Metformin alone could be considered for cycle regulation, with limited supporting evidence from six studies [185 adolescents]. Four studies (142 adolescents) support considering metformin over COCP for metabolic features and COCP over metformin for hirsutism and/or irregular cycles. Among women with a body mass index < 30 kg/m2, combining COCPs with metformin adds minimal benefit; adolescent data are absent. Evidence from 26 studies, including two adolescent studies using antiandrogens together with two insulin sensitizers, indicates a limited role for antiandrogens. No adolescent-specific recommendations were made for anti-obesity drugs or cosmetic therapies because adolescent data are lacking. Anti-obesity drugs nevertheless have beneficial effects in people with obesity and some supporting PCOS evidence. Eight adult PCOS studies support laser and light therapy for hirsutism and associated psychological features. Inositol preparations cannot currently be recommended for adolescents: adolescent data are absent, and adult PCOS evidence has demonstrated only biochemical efficacy. Table 4 details treatment choices, cautions, and grades.

document_sections.heading: Models of care and transition
document_sections.content: Evidence about care models for women and adolescents with PCOS is limited, and Table 4 provides general considerations. Only one qualitative study examined transition to adult care. Adolescents with PCOS or “at risk” need longitudinal follow-up and an appropriate transfer to adult services. Some have gone several years without contact with healthcare professionals, during which obesity, dysglycemia, dyslipidemia, depression, and subfertility often progress. Reliable information sources, including the free AskPCOS app, are therefore important. Before transfer, clinicians and adolescents should discuss comorbidities and devise lifelong plans. Shared decisions and education about care needs aim to build adolescents' ability to manage their own health. Transition should be planned to sustain high-quality care and increase responsibility for self-care.

document_sections.heading: Discussion
document_sections.content: This manuscript draws together adolescent-specific recommendations from the 2023 International Evidence-based PCOS Guideline. International participation, rigorous evidence-based methods, and independent review underlie the Guideline. Fewer recommendations address adolescents than adults because adolescent PCOS research is limited. Normal pubertal features overlap with adult criteria, creating risks of delayed diagnosis, underdiagnosis, and overdiagnosis. Although evidence supports PCOM and AMH as adult diagnostic features, neither should be used for adolescent diagnosis because of overdiagnosis risk; they can be used at approximately 8 years postmenarche when axis maturation and evidence-based PCOM criteria permit assessment. Adolescent diagnosis instead combines time-defined menstrual irregularity with clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism after other disorders are excluded. These criteria are intended to support timely diagnosis, earlier identification of adolescents at considerable risk of weight gain and diabetes, screening and management of long-term metabolic risks, and optimization of future fertility outcomes. An adolescent with either feature alone can be considered “at risk,” avoiding an inappropriate definitive label without allowing delayed diagnosis to go unaddressed. Such adolescents need symptom-directed care and continuing follow-up. Families and adolescents should discuss when reassessment will occur, particularly across transition; PCOS can be diagnosed before 8 years postmenarche if both features emerge. Re-evaluation before and after transfer is therefore essential. Recent data suggest abnormal metabolic profiles among adolescents “at risk,” but prospective comparisons with healthy adolescents are needed to establish follow-up timing and future PCOS risk. Evidence supports routine screening and management of depression in adolescents with PCOS. Adolescents have reported inadequate emotional support and education; more research is needed on emotional wellbeing strategies, anxiety, quality of life, body image, and eating disorders. A lifelong plan should include age-appropriate education, healthy lifestyles, timely metabolic screening, reproductive planning, and adult-care transition, with shared decisions directed by adolescent concerns. The Guideline recommends COCP for menstrual irregularity and hyperandrogenism in adolescents with PCOS or “at risk,” with the lowest effective estrogen dose; no particular progestin, estrogen, dose, or COCP combination can currently be recommended. Absolute and relative contraindications require consideration under the World Health Organization Medical Eligibility Criteria. When an adolescent “at risk” receives COCP, the adolescent and parents should be advised that diagnostic reassessment may require at least 3-month withdrawal, especially without hyperandrogenism and where hypogonadism is possible. Metformin is recommended for metabolic features and cycle regulation in adolescents with PCOS or “at risk.” Insulin resistance is difficult to assess: it is most common with higher BMI but can occur at normal BMI, where metformin has also been beneficial. Further adolescent studies should examine contraception preferences, hair-reduction methods, antiandrogens, antiobesity drugs, and weight management. Declared strengths are broad international involvement of consumers and multidisciplinary clinicians, methods aligned with AGREE-II, detailed evidence synthesis and integrity checks, independent high-quality appraisal, and a multifaceted international implementation program. Declared limitations include priorities established mainly by women rather than adolescents, although emerging adolescent findings suggest similar priorities apart from infertility. Despite more adolescent studies, studies restricted to adolescents, defining the postmenarcheal interval, or using current diagnostic criteria remain few and of limited quality. Research priorities include well-defined adolescent cohorts, PCOS natural history, emotional wellbeing, optimal treatment, weight strategies, care models, and transition. Adult recommendations may apply where adolescent studies are unavailable, but their use needs to account for adolescence.

document_sections.heading: Conclusions
document_sections.content: The adolescent-specific recommendations of the 2023 International Evidence-based PCOS Guideline establish diagnostic criteria that differ from adult criteria and are intended to improve diagnostic accuracy and timeliness. They emphasize identifying and managing adolescents “at risk,” screening adolescents with PCOS for depression and glucose abnormalities, responding to adolescents' priorities, and preparing a lifelong health plan. The overall evidence remains limited and of low to moderate quality, making further research during adolescence and longer-term follow-up a priority.
